title: Kurma
hook: the mountain starts to sink, and a tortoise dives under it
tomorrow: they churn for nectar. so why does poison come up first?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Matsya dove after the stolen Vedas and brought them home, and the fish's week closed. The gods need a mountain to churn the sea. Who holds it up?

Tug-of-war at a school field day: two teams, one rope, everyone straining, and then the ground under the middle starts to give. Now make it enormous. A mountain, set point-down into the sea for a churning stick. A great serpent wound around it for a rope. The gods hauling one end, the asuras the other, back and forth, the way a churn turns milk to butter. It's working. And then the mountain begins to sink.
screen: `ONE ROPE, TWO TEAMS.` → `A MOUNTAIN FOR A CHURNING STICK.` → `THE MOUNTAIN SINKS.`

segments.voice: This is the churning of the ocean of milk. In the Vishnu Purana, the gods have lost their strength after a sage's curse, and Vishnu tells them how to win it back: churn the ocean for amrita, the nectar of immortality. They can't do it alone, so they work with the asuras, their rivals, and promise them a share. The mountain is Mandara; the rope is the serpent Vasuki. But a mountain has no floor to stand on in the middle of the sea. So Vishnu comes down a second time, now as a vast tortoise, Kurma. He dives under the mountain and takes it on his back, and the churning goes on, turning on his shell. Notice what this descent does. The fish swam and towed and dove. The tortoise doesn't pull the rope or fight anyone. He holds. All the action is above him: gods and asuras straining, the sea foaming. Underneath, unseen, the one thing keeping it from failing is something steady to stand on. And a detail worth telling someone tonight: in this story, the gods and their rivals are on the same rope, and the work needs both ends.
screen: `THE OCEAN OF MILK.` · `GODS AND ASURAS ON ONE ROPE.` · `THE MOUNTAIN NEEDS A FLOOR.` · then, large: `KURMA HOLDS FROM BELOW.`

segments.voice: Sit so your back is supported, by a chair, a wall or the floor. Let it take your whole weight, the way the tortoise takes the mountain, and notice each place where you're held. If you pray, you can rest your weight in God.
Kurma: the tortoise, Vishnu's second descent, who holds the mountain while the sea is churned.
Your line: Kurma. All the action above, and the tortoise holding from below. Until tomorrow.
